questions.question: A definition has balanced parentheses, a present else branch, and consistent indentation, but applies (+) to a Bool and an Int. Which stage catches this, and what is it called?
options: Syntax analysis catches it, as a syntax error
Type analysis catches it, as a type error
Evaluation catches it, at run time
Nothing catches it — GHC would silently coerce the Bool to an Int
questions.explanation: The structure of the expression is fine (it parses), so syntax analysis passes. But (+) requires both arguments to be of the same Num-constrained type, and Bool is not a Num instance, so type analysis rejects it before any evaluation begins.
optionFeedback: Syntax analysis only checks structure/shape — parentheses, keywords, layout. This expression parses just fine; the problem only shows up when types are checked.
Correct. The expression is syntactically well-formed but ill-typed, so it is rejected in the type-analysis stage, before evaluation.
Evaluation never begins, because the expression fails the type stage first — that's the whole point of the two-stage gate.
Haskell has no implicit coercion between Bool and Int; there is no numeric interpretation of True or False to fall back on, so this is rejected outright.

questions.question: Why does a type error 'prevent evaluation entirely', even for the parts of the program that don't involve the error?
options: It doesn't — GHC runs whatever it can and skips the broken part
Because a module must pass both syntax and type analysis as a whole before GHC will run any of it; a single type error stops the module from loading at all
Because type errors are warnings, not errors, so they only affect performance
Because Haskell evaluates lazily, so type errors are simply postponed until the last line runs
questions.explanation: GHC checks an entire module before running anything in it. If any definition fails to type check, the module does not load, and nothing in it — including unrelated, perfectly correct functions — gets to run. This is why 'is it well typed?' has to be asked before 'what value does it produce?'.
optionFeedback: GHC does not selectively skip ill-typed definitions and run the rest — the whole module must type check before ghci will load it or a program will compile.
Correct — type checking is whole-module, so one ill-typed definition blocks the entire module from being accepted, regardless of what else in it is fine.
A type error is a hard error, not a warning — it stops compilation/loading outright, not merely a performance note.
Laziness postpones *evaluation* of well-typed expressions until their value is needed; it has nothing to do with type checking, which happens statically, before any evaluation at all.

questions.question: head [] compiles without complaint but crashes when run. Which class of error is this, and why does it slip past compilation?
options: Syntax error — head is spelled correctly but used wrongly

Semantic error — head :: [a] -> a type checks against any list argument, including an empty one, so nothing about the types is wrong; the failure is about meaning (there is no first element), and only shows up once the empty list actually reaches head
It is not an error at all, since Haskell allows empty lists
Type error — [a] and [] are different types
questions.explanation: head [] is a semantic error: everything type checks (head really does accept any [a], including []), so GHC has no basis to reject it. The problem is a meaning-level one — head is undefined on an empty list — and it can only be detected by actually running the program and reaching that call.
optionFeedback: head is used with entirely correct syntax and the correct type of argument (a list); nothing about the structure or naming is wrong.
Correct. This is the standard example of a semantic error: well-typed, well-formed, and wrong only in what it means to ask for the first element of nothing.
It is a genuine, well-documented run-time error (Prelude.head: empty list) — Haskell allows the empty list as a value, but head is a partial function that is not defined on it.
[] is perfectly compatible with type [a] for any a (it's the empty list of that type) — there is no type mismatch here at all.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on separating 'syntax error' (narrow sense) from 'type error', even though both stop compilation?
options: It doesn't matter — they are the same thing under a different name

Because the fix is different: a syntax error means the parser couldn't build an expression at all (check brackets/keywords/layout), while a type error means the expression parsed fine but the types don't line up (check which subexpression should have which type)
Because type errors are actually run-time errors
Because GHC reports them with the exact same message
questions.explanation: The two need different remedies, which is why Section 3's diagnostic table asks a different question for each: for a syntax error, 'is an else missing, are the parentheses balanced'; for a type error, 'which subexpression must produce Bool'. Knowing which one you have tells you where to look.
optionFeedback: They are different stages (Section 1's diagram) with different causes and different fixes, even though both happen before evaluation.
Correct — this is exactly why Section 3 gives each its own diagnostic question: a syntax error is fixed by repairing structure, a type error by finding the mismatched subexpression.
Type errors are caught in the type-analysis stage, strictly before evaluation ever starts — they are compile-time, not run-time.
GHC's messages are distinctive — 'parse error on input' for a syntax error versus 'Couldn't match expected type' for a type error, as Section 3's table shows.

questions.question: GHC reports No instance for (Num a). What category is this, and what should you check first?
options: Syntax — check for a missing else
Scope — check the spelling of a variable name
Class constraint — check which typeclass the operation needs, and whether it appears before => in the signature
Semantic — check whether the recursion terminates
questions.explanation: No instance for (...) messages report a missing typeclass constraint — here, some numeric operation is being used on a type parameter that was never declared Num. The fix is to add the required constraint before => in the type signature.
optionFeedback: A missing else produces 'parse error on input', a structural complaint — this message is about typeclasses, not parsing.
A scope error looks like 'Variable not in scope: x' and is about names, not about which operations a type supports.
Correct. 'No instance for' names a missing constraint — the fix is adding it (e.g. Num a =>) to the signature.
Semantic errors are run-time failures (head [], divide by zero, ...); 'No instance for' is a compile-time message, caught before anything runs.

questions.question: A program compiles cleanly but the ghci session hangs and never returns a prompt. Which category, and what's the first thing to check?
options: Type error — check the type signature
Semantic error — check whether the recursive argument is actually shrinking towards the base case
Syntax error — check for unbalanced parentheses
Scope error — check for a misspelled variable
questions.explanation: A hang is a run-time (semantic) failure: the program compiled and started running, but the recursion never reaches its base case — exactly the non-terminating fac (-1) style of fault from Chapter 5.
optionFeedback: A type problem would be caught before the session even starts running; 'compiles cleanly' rules this out.
Correct — hanging is a semantic, run-time symptom, and the standard cause is recursion that never reaches its base case.
Unbalanced parentheses would be caught at the syntax stage and the module wouldn't load in the first place — it wouldn't get as far as hanging.
A misspelled variable produces 'Variable not in scope', caught before running; it wouldn't compile cleanly in the first place.

questions.question: Why did isDigitBad pass isDigitBad '5' but fail isDigitBad '0' and isDigitBad '9'?
options: Because '5' is not actually a digit
Because isDigitBad uses strict inequalities (< instead of <=), which correctly include interior digits like '5' but wrongly exclude the two digits that sit exactly on the boundary
Because ghci evaluates '0' and '9' differently from other characters
Because absoluteValue and isDigitBad share the same bug
questions.explanation: '0' < '0' is False (a value is never strictly less than itself), so isDigitBad '0' fails even though '0' is a digit. The same happens at '9' via c < '9'. Interior digits like '5' satisfy both strict inequalities, so only the boundary values expose the fault.
optionFeedback: '5' is a perfectly ordinary decimal digit — the point is that the bug is invisible on ordinary digits and only shows up at the two edges.
Correct. Strict < excludes the endpoints, so isDigitBad wrongly rejects exactly the two digits that sit on the boundary of its own comparison.
ghci evaluates every Char comparison the same way, by character code — there's nothing special happening to '0' or '9' in the evaluator itself.
They are unrelated examples illustrating the same general principle (test the boundary), not the same bug in the same function.

questions.question: For a function f :: [a] -> b, which set of test inputs best follows the 'test by type' guidance in this section?
options: [1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9] — three normal-looking lists
[] (empty), a singleton like [1], and a list of two or more elements like [1,2,3]
Just one very long list, to stress-test performance
[1,2,3] tested three times, to rule out non-determinism
questions.explanation: The 'Boundaries worth testing by type' table specifically calls out [], a singleton, and a list of two-or-more for list arguments — these are the shapes where list-processing code most often mishandles a case (an empty pattern match, an off-by-one on a one-element list, or general recursion).
optionFeedback: Three lists of the same shape (all length 3, all normal) test the same case three times — they miss the empty-list and singleton edges entirely.
Correct — this is exactly the list row of the boundary table: empty, singleton, and 2+ elements are the shapes where list functions most often break.
Performance is not what boundary testing targets here; a single long list also doesn't touch the empty or singleton edge cases at all.
Haskell functions are pure — the same input always gives the same output, so repeating an identical test cannot reveal anything a single run wouldn't.

questions.question: A function compiles and runs, but gives the wrong answer on some inputs. Which step of the procedure applies, and what should you do?
options: Step 1 — read the message more carefully, there must be one
Step 4 — compare against the specification: since it compiles and runs, the fault is in the formula, not the syntax or types, so return to the specification's examples and dry run the failing input
Step 2 — classify it as a syntax error
Step 5 — silence it with a catch-all pattern
questions.explanation: If it compiles and runs, both compile-time gates (syntax, type) already passed, and it isn't crashing, so it isn't a semantic run-time exception either. What's left is that the formula itself computes the wrong value — exactly what Step 4 is for, and exactly the situation in Section 2's Practice question 7.
optionFeedback: There is no error message here at all — the program ran to completion and simply produced a wrong value. Step 1 doesn't apply when nothing failed to compile or crashed.
Correct. A wrong-but-running answer means the fault is in the logic (the formula), which is precisely what Step 4 directs you to check against the specification.
A syntax error would have prevented the program from compiling in the first place — it can't be classified as one if it already compiled and ran.
Adding a catch-all doesn't fix a wrong formula, and Step 5 explicitly warns against silencing symptoms rather than fixing causes — it also isn't about a non-crashing wrong answer at all.

questions.question: Why does Step 3 recommend entering parts of a failing expression at the ghci prompt separately, rather than just re-reading the whole thing?
options: It doesn't help — the whole expression must always be tested as one unit
Because checking sub-expressions individually with :type narrows down exactly which piece disagrees with your expectation, rather than guessing across the whole expression at once
Because ghci cannot evaluate whole expressions, only fragments
Because it avoids having to read the error message at all
questions.explanation: This is a standard bisection strategy: instead of staring at a large failing expression, you isolate the smallest failing subexpression by testing pieces individually. :type on each piece tells you exactly where the type you expected and the type GHC infers diverge.
optionFeedback: Breaking a large expression into testable pieces is exactly the point of this step — it isolates where the disagreement is, rather than treating the whole expression as an opaque unit.
Correct — this is a bisection approach: narrow down which specific subexpression is responsible, rather than treating the whole failing line as a single mystery.
ghci evaluates whole expressions perfectly well; the recommendation to test fragments is a diagnostic strategy, not a technical limitation of ghci.
Step 1 already asked you to read the message; Step 3 is a follow-up strategy for when the message alone doesn't pinpoint the fault, not a way to skip reading it.

check-converting-run-time-failures-to-co.title: Check: converting run-time failures to compile-time ones

questions.question: Which change converts head []'s run-time crash into something the type checker can flag instead?
options: :set -Wincomplete-patterns, since head's problem is a missing pattern
Changing the function that calls head to match [] itself first, or to work with a Maybe-returning alternative instead of the partial head
Adding deriving (Show) to the list type
Nothing can be done — head's precondition can never be checked before run time
questions.explanation: head is partial: it simply has no equation for []. -Wincomplete-patterns helps for functions *you* write with missing patterns, but head itself is a library function whose partiality you cannot annotate away. The fix is at the call site: pattern-match [] yourself, or use a total alternative that returns Maybe, so the empty case is handled — or visible in the type — before the crash can happen.
optionFeedback: -Wincomplete-patterns flags missing equations in functions you define; it cannot retroactively add a case to Prelude's own head, which is inherently partial.
Correct — since you can't fix head itself, the fix moves to wherever head is called: handle [] explicitly, or use a Maybe-returning function so the empty case is forced into the type.
deriving (Show) only affects how values are printed to text; it has nothing to do with head's partiality on the empty list.

It can be prevented — this is exactly what widening a partial function into a total one (Section 2's Callout) means: convert it into something the compiler, or at least an explicit pattern match, catches first.

questions.question: read s :: Integer throws Prelude.read: no parse on bad input. What is the recommended prevention, and why doesn't -Wincomplete-patterns help here?
options: Validate the input text before parsing it — -Wincomplete-patterns only warns about missing equations in your own pattern matches, not about whether arbitrary text denotes a valid value
There is no way to prevent this failure
Use :set -Wincomplete-patterns, since read is missing a pattern for invalid text
Rename the variable to avoid the scope error
questions.explanation: read's failure isn't a missing pattern in code you wrote — it's a property of the input string itself, checked only when read actually tries to parse it. -Wincomplete-patterns cannot see into a String's contents at compile time; the only prevention is to validate the text (or use a safe-read alternative) before calling read.
optionFeedback: Correct. The fix targeted at this specific failure is validating the input before parsing — a compiler flag about incomplete pattern matches can't inspect the contents of a String.
Section 6's table lists a concrete prevention for this exact failure: validate before parsing.
-Wincomplete-patterns checks whether your equations/guards cover every constructor shape of an argument's type — it has no way to know which strings look like valid Integer literals.
There is no scope error anywhere in this example — the fault is that the text can't be parsed as the target type, which is a different category entirely.
